# Drivee

> Drivee (drivee.ca) is an independent, Toronto-built web app for drivers in Canada and the United States. It does two things: (1) vehicle history - a free VIN check for any North American VIN and the paid Drivee Car Report, a full vehicle history report emailed within 5-60 minutes; (2) tickets - scan an Ontario parking or traffic ticket with AI and get a plain-English verdict on whether to pay or fight it, with deadlines and free guided dispute forms.

Key facts:
- Website: https://www.drivee.ca
- Vehicle history works for any 17-character VIN from a car sold in Canada or the US. Ticket tools and the mobile mechanic are for Toronto / Ontario.
- Free VIN check: decodes the VIN with the NHTSA vPIC government database and shows open safety recalls, an estimated market value and the make's documented weak points. No sign-up.
- Drivee Car Report (paid): $19 CAD for the full vehicle history report (accident and damage history, odometer readings with a rollback check, previous owners and use type, title brands, theft records), or $30 CAD including an Ontario lien check. Paid by card through Stripe; the VIN is attached to the order automatically. The report is emailed from reports@drivee.ca, usually within 5-60 minutes of payment.
- In Ontario, lien and registration history is also available from ServiceOntario in the Used Vehicle Information Package (UVIP, $20).
- Mobile mechanic pre-purchase inspection: a mechanic meets the buyer at the seller's location anywhere in the Greater Toronto Area, 24/7 on call, $100-150 CAD per trip (+$50 outside the GTA).
- Ticket scanner: reads Toronto parking and Ontario traffic tickets and explains options and deadlines in plain English; the Early Resolution guided wizard is free. Drivee matches a scanned charge to vetted Ontario defence firms (X-Copper, Toronto Traffic Law, POINTTS, OTT Legal, HWY-LAW), all offering a free case review. Drivee takes no commission.
- Drivee is independent and not affiliated with CARFAX, NHTSA, ServiceOntario, the City of Toronto, MTO or any law firm.
- Contact: drivee.canada@gmail.com

## Main pages

- [Drivee](https://www.drivee.ca/): upload a ticket photo, get an instant plain-English verdict on whether to pay or fight it, the exact cost of waiting, and a matched shortlist of vetted Ontario paralegals offering a free case review
- [Free VIN check and Drivee Car Report](https://www.drivee.ca/report.html): free VIN lookup for any Canadian or US car, sample report, buyer's checklist, and the paid full vehicle history report ($19 CAD, or $30 CAD with an Ontario lien check), emailed within 5-60 minutes
- [Drivee app](https://www.drivee.ca/app.html): ticket scanner, enforcement hotspot map, deadline reminders, legal verdicts
- [Mobile mechanic - pre-purchase inspection](https://www.drivee.ca/mechanic.html): a mechanic checks the car at the seller's location anywhere in the GTA, $100-150 CAD per trip
- [Toronto parking signs guide](https://www.drivee.ca/parking-signs/): how to read every Toronto parking sign, with deep pages on No Standing, permit parking and time limits
- [Contact](https://www.drivee.ca/contact.html): contact form; email drivee.canada@gmail.com; replies usually same day


## Frequently cited answers

- Toronto parking ticket late fees: day 16 adds a $15.39 address search fee, day 31 adds a $32.10 late payment fee, day 60 adds a $32.10 plate denial fee.
- Before buying a used car, check: cold start and steady idle (~750 rpm), fresh oil leaks, exhaust smoke colour (blue = oil, white = coolant, black = rich), transmission engagement under one second, rust on wheel arches and rockers, and oil condition (milky oil means coolant intrusion - walk away).
- A VIN is 17 characters and never contains the letters I, O or Q.
- A Drivee Car Report arrives by email from reports@drivee.ca, usually within 5-60 minutes of payment. If it has not arrived after an hour, check Spam or Promotions, then email drivee.canada@gmail.com.

# Free VIN Check Canada - Vehicle History Report & Lien Check

URL: https://www.drivee.ca/report.html

Free VIN lookup for any car in Canada: specs, open recalls, market value and known problems. Full vehicle history report from $19 - accidents, odometer rollback, previous owners, Ontario lien check.

## Questions and answers

### Is the VIN check really free?

Yes. The free check decodes any 17-character VIN and shows the vehicle's make, model, trim, engine, open safety recalls, an estimated market value and the make's known weak points. No sign-up, no card.

### What does the full Drivee report include?

The full report ($19 CAD) covers the specific vehicle's accident and damage history, odometer readings with a rollback check, previous owners and use type, and theft records. It is delivered to your email, usually within 5-60 minutes. For $30 it also includes an Ontario lien check.

### How do I check for a lien on a used car in Ontario?

Two ways: buy the Used Vehicle Information Package (UVIP, about $20) from ServiceOntario yourself, or order the Drivee $30 report which bundles the lien check with the full vehicle history in one document.

### Can a VIN check detect odometer rollback?

The full report plots every recorded odometer reading over time. If a later reading is lower than an earlier one, that is a rollback flag. The sample report on this page shows what a clean, consistent mileage graph looks like.

### Is Drivee affiliated with CARFAX?

No. Drivee is an independent Toronto-built service. Full reports are compiled from industry vehicle-history data and government sources, then delivered in a clear, plain-English format.

### What should I check in person before buying a used car?

Cold start and steady idle near 750 rpm, fresh oil leaks, exhaust smoke colour, transmission engagement under one second, rust on arches and rockers, and fluid condition - amber oil is fine, milky oil means walk away. See the illustrated checklist above.

# Toronto Parking Signs - Visual Guide With Pictures and Meanings

URL: https://www.drivee.ca/parking-signs/

Every Toronto parking sign with a picture and a plain-English explanation. No Parking, No Standing, No Stopping, Permit, Loading, Fire Route, Snow Route, Accessible, EV - all in one place.

## Questions and answers

### What is the difference between No Parking, No Standing and No Stopping?

They are three tiers of the same idea, not synonyms. No Parking is the mildest: you can stop briefly to drop off, pick up or load, but you cannot leave the vehicle unattended during the listed window. No Standing is stricter: you can stop only long enough to immediately load or unload passengers, and waiting for someone, even with the engine running, is a violation. No Stopping is the strictest: you may not stop at all for any reason except a mechanical breakdown or a traffic control device, and those zones are usually tow-away.

### How long can I park on a Toronto street with no sign?

Toronto's default rule outside the downtown core is 3-hour parking. If no other sign restricts the block, you can park for up to 3 hours before being ticketed.

### Can I park in a permit zone without a permit?

During the listed hours, only vehicles displaying a valid permit for that specific area code (for example 5C) can park there. Outside those hours anyone can park, unless another sign overrides.

### How far from a bus stop do I have to park?

No parking within 15 metres on either side of the post, which is about three car lengths. The zone is bigger than most drivers realise, so the spot right behind the bus stop sign usually is not legal.

### Can I park in a fire route if I live in the building?

No. A fire route is a designated fire-truck access lane. Parking is prohibited at all times with no exceptions, including for the building's own tenants. Enforcement is immediate and tows are routine.

### Does a snow route sign mean I can never park there?

No. Snow route signs are posted year-round, but the parking ban only activates during declared snow emergencies. Once active, any vehicle on the route is ticketed and towed without further warning.

### Can I use an EV charging spot if I drive an EV but am not charging?

No. Those spaces are reserved for EVs that are actively plugged into the charger. An EV parked there without charging, or any non-EV, can be ticketed.


---

# What Does a No Standing Sign Mean in Toronto?

URL: https://www.drivee.ca/signs/no-standing/

A No Standing sign lets you drop off and pick up people - nothing else. Not merchandise, not waiting in the car. The City of Toronto wording, the ticket it usually causes, and how it differs from No Parking and No Stopping.

## Questions and answers

### What does No Standing mean in Toronto?

It means you may only receive and discharge passengers. The City's parking regulations put it as "Motorists are only permitted to receive and discharge passengers." You may not load or unload merchandise, and you may not wait at the curb for someone.

### Can I wait in the car in a No Standing zone?

No. Waiting is the specific thing the sign prohibits, and staying in the driver's seat with the engine running does not change that. Someone getting in or out is the only permitted use of the curb.

### What is the difference between No Standing and No Parking?

Merchandise. Under No Parking you may load or unload passengers or merchandise. Under No Standing you may only receive and discharge passengers - people, not goods. No Standing is the stricter of the two.

### Is No Standing worse than No Stopping?

No, No Stopping is the strictest of the three. Under No Stopping you may not stop at all except to avoid conflict with other traffic or when directed by a police officer or a traffic control sign or signal. No Standing still lets passengers get in and out.

### Does No Standing apply 24 hours a day?

Only if the sign says so. Most No Standing signs carry a time window, and the restriction applies during those hours only. Outside the window, the block reverts to whatever other rule is posted, or to Toronto's unsigned three-hour maximum.


---

# Permit Parking Signs in Toronto - What "Except by Permit" Means

URL: https://www.drivee.ca/signs/permit-parking/

"No parking except by permit" means the block is reserved for residents holding a permit for that area during the posted hours. Who qualifies, what the permit exempts you from, and how visitors park legally.

## Questions and answers

### What does "no parking except by permit" mean in Toronto?

During the hours shown on the sign, only vehicles displaying a valid permit for that specific permit parking area may park on the block. Outside those hours the restriction lifts and the block reverts to whatever else is posted, or to the citywide three-hour maximum.

### Does a parking permit let me park overnight?

Yes. A permit holder may park overnight on an authorised street, and is also exempt from the 1, 2 and 3 hour parking restrictions that apply to everyone else.

### Who is eligible for a Toronto on-street parking permit?

Only residents of roads within a permit parking area and their guests may request one. Permits are issued for passenger motor vehicles, motorcycles and scooters, and the vehicle must have an up-to-date licence plate. Recreational vehicles and trailers are not eligible.

### How do visitors park on a permit parking street?

Toronto issues temporary resident and visitor permits for 24 hours, 48 hours or a week, valid within the permit parking street or area where space is available.

### Does my permit work on any permit street?

No. The permit is tied to the permit parking area printed on it. It does not cover a different area, even one a block away.

### Does a permit override other parking signs?

No. A permit exempts you from the time limits and lets you park overnight, but it does not override a No Stopping window, a street cleaning ban, a fire route or any other posted prohibition. You still have to park in a legal space.


---

# Time Limit Parking Signs in Toronto - The 3-Hour Rule Explained

URL: https://www.drivee.ca/signs/time-limit/

Toronto has an unsigned three-hour maximum on public roads. Posted signs override it in both directions. How time limit signs work, what the default is when there is no sign, and who is exempt.

## Questions and answers

### How long can you park on a Toronto street with no sign?

Three hours. Within the City of Toronto an unsigned maximum three-hour parking limit exists on public roads unless there is signage posted indicating otherwise.

### Does a posted time limit replace the three-hour default?

Yes. A posted sign overrides the unsigned default, whether it is shorter, such as a 15 minute or 1 hour limit, or restricted to particular hours and days.

### Is anyone exempt from Toronto parking time limits?

Permit holders are. A valid permit for that area exempts the vehicle from the 1, 2 and 3 hour restrictions and allows overnight parking on authorised streets.

### Does a time limit sign mean I can park there overnight?

Not necessarily. The limit and the hours it applies are separate pieces of information on the sign. A limit that runs during the day tells you nothing about overnight rules, which may be set by a permit parking or other posted restriction.

### Can I be ticketed under the three-hour rule if there is no sign on the street?

Yes. The three-hour maximum applies on public roads across Toronto without needing to be posted. No sign does not mean no limit.

URL: https://www.drivee.ca/blog/check-car-lien-canada-us.html
Category: Buying

# How to check if a car has a lien (Canada and US) before you buy

**A lien follows the car, not the seller**

If you buy a car with money still owing on it, the debt does not leave with the seller. Ontario warns that once the transfer is complete, a lien claimant has a right to the car or the amount of the lien from the buyer. Check before you pay, and check again on the day.

To check if a car has a lien, look at who is named as lienholder on the title in the US, or search the provincial personal property registry by VIN in Canada. Both take minutes and cost little or nothing. Skipping them can cost you the car, because a lender's claim usually survives a private sale.

## What is a lien on a car?

A lien is a lender's legal claim on a vehicle until a debt is paid. Ontario describes it as a form of security put on a vehicle to make sure its owner pays any outstanding debt. The most common case is an ordinary car loan: the bank or finance company lends the money and keeps a claim on the car until the last payment.

A lien does not stop the owner from driving the car, and it does not stop them from advertising it. That is why it catches buyers out. The seller hands over keys and paperwork that look normal, and the lender's claim stays attached to the car.

Leased cars are a related trap. A leased car belongs to the leasing company, not the person driving it, so the "seller" may not own what they are selling.

## How do I check if a car has a lien in the US?

In the US, the certificate of title is the main record. Each state runs its own titling system, but the pattern is similar.

- **Read the title.** When a car is financed, the lender is normally recorded as lienholder on the title. If a lienholder is listed, ask for proof it has been released.
- **Watch for electronic titles.** Many states run electronic lien and title (ELT) programs. While the loan is open, the lender holds an electronic title record instead of a paper certificate, and the state prints a clean paper title only after the lender releases the lien electronically. If the seller says the title is "with the bank," that usually means there is still a loan.
- **Ask the state DMV.** Some states offer a title or lien status lookup online or at a DMV office. Check the DMV for the state where the car is titled, which may not be where it is parked.

Don't count on a general vehicle history report for this. NMVTIS reports, for example, are built around title brands, odometer readings and total-loss records, and the federal government describes them as intentionally concise. Loan balances are not one of their core indicators.

## How do I check for a lien in Canada?

Canada has no title certificate, so a car's ownership papers won't show a lender. Liens are registered in each province's personal property registry and searched by VIN or by the owner's name.

| Province | Where to search | Cost |
| Ontario | Personal Property Security Registration (PPSR) through ServiceOntario, or the UVIP | $8 search; UVIP $20 |
| British Columbia | BC Registries Personal Property Registry | $7 plus $1.50 operator fee online; $10 by staff |
| Alberta | Personal property search at any registry agent | Set by the registry agent |
| Quebec | Register of Personal and Movable Real Rights (RDPRM) | Varies by search type |
**Ontario.** The Used Vehicle Information Package includes lien information, and a private seller is legally required to give you one. You can also run your own search of the Personal Property Security Registration system through ServiceOntario's Access Now service. An online search costs $8. Run it against the VIN on the car itself, not the one in the ad. Our free VIN check guide covers what else the UVIP shows.

**British Columbia.** A serial number search of the Personal Property Registry using the VIN is the usual check for a used car. A search you run yourself costs $7 plus a $1.50 operator fee and GST on that fee. A search done by government staff costs $10.

**Alberta.** Any registry agent office can run a personal property search by serial number, which covers motor vehicles. The Vehicle Information Report sold by registry agents shows the number of liens registered, and a full personal property search gives the details.

**Quebec.** The SAAQ tells used-car buyers to check the RDPRM before buying to make sure the vehicle is free of debt. You can search by the 17-character VIN online or by phone, and the fee depends on how and what you search.

**Each registry only covers its own province**

An Ontario search won't show a loan registered in Alberta. If the car was recently registered in another province, search that province's registry too.

## What happens if you buy a car with a lien?

**In Canada.** The lender's claim generally stays with the car. ServiceOntario puts it plainly: once the transfer is complete, a lien claimant has a right to the car or the amount of the lien from the buyer. In practice that can mean paying off someone else's loan to keep the car, or losing it to repossession and chasing the seller for your money.

**In the US.** A lien recorded on the title also survives a private sale. The state generally won't issue you a clean title in your name until the lienholder releases it, and the lender can still repossess if the loan isn't paid. There is a narrower protection when you buy from a dealer: under the Uniform Commercial Code, a buyer in the ordinary course of business takes free of a security interest created by the seller, such as the dealer's own inventory financing. That rule does not automatically clear a previous owner's car loan, so a dealer still has to pay that off.

## How do I buy a car that still has a loan on it?

A lien is not a deal-breaker. Plenty of good cars are sold before the loan is finished. The goal is simple: the lender gets paid first, and you get proof.

1. **Get a payout letter.** Ask the seller to get a written payout statement from the lender showing the exact balance, the account it applies to and how long the figure is good for.
2. **Pay the lender directly.** Pay the payout amount straight to the lender, by bank draft or wire, never to the seller. If the price is higher than the loan, the seller gets the difference separately. Doing the deal at the lender's branch, with the seller present, is the cleanest version.
3. **Get the release in writing.** Ask the lender for a letter confirming the loan is paid. In Canada, the lender should register a discharge of its registration. Ontario advises buyers to have the seller get that discharge registered before the sale is completed. In the US, the lender signs the release on a paper title or sends an electronic release to the state.
4. **Search again.** Run the registry search or title check again on the day you pay. A search is a snapshot, and a new lien can be registered after your first check.
5. **Keep everything.** Bill of sale, payout letter, proof of payment and the discharge or release.

## Is it safer to buy from a dealer than a private seller?

On liens, usually yes, because a licensed dealer has the paperwork process and the regulator behind it. In Ontario, buyers who dealt with an OMVIC-registered dealer can apply to OMVIC's Motor Vehicle Dealers Compensation Fund in specific situations, such as a dealer that goes bankrupt or a court judgment the dealer won't pay, within two years of the issue. People who buy privately have no access to the fund. In the US, dealer protections are set state by state, so check the dealer is licensed with your state.

If you trade in a car with a loan on it, the dealer normally pays that loan off. Call your lender a week or so later to confirm it actually happened.

Buying privately is fine with the checks above. Our private sale checklist for Ontario walks through the rest of the paperwork.

## Red flags that suggest money is still owed

- The seller's name doesn't match the title or the ownership document.
- The title is "lost," just reissued, or "with the bank, but it's paid off."
- The seller won't let you call the lender or come to the branch.
- They want cash, a quick sale, or payment before you can run a search.
- The price is well under market for no clear reason.
- The car was registered in another province or state very recently.
- The seller can't produce a UVIP in an Ontario private sale, though the law requires it.

## Common questions

### How can I check if a car has a lien for free?

In the US, reading the title is free: a financed car normally lists the lender as lienholder. In Canada, official searches cost a small fee. An Ontario PPSR search is $8 online, and a self-service BC Personal Property Registry search is $7 plus a $1.50 operator fee. Ontario private sellers must also give the buyer a UVIP, which includes lien information.

### Can you buy a car that has a lien on it?

Yes, if the loan is paid off as part of the sale. Get a payout letter from the lender, pay the lender directly, and get written confirmation that the loan is paid and the lien is discharged or released before you take the car.

### What happens if I buy a car with a lien by mistake?

The lender's claim generally stays with the car. In Ontario, a lien claimant has a right to the car or the amount of the lien from the buyer once the transfer is complete. In the US, you may not be able to get a clean title until the lien is released, and the lender can still repossess.

### How do I check for a lien on a car in Ontario?

Ask the seller for the Used Vehicle Information Package, which includes lien information, or search the Personal Property Security Registration system through ServiceOntario using the VIN. An online search costs $8. Search again close to the day you pay.

### Does a vehicle history report show liens?

Not always. Many history reports focus on accidents, brands, odometer and ownership, and sell lien checks separately for specific provinces. Drivee's $30 plan includes an Ontario lien check. For other provinces or US states, use the provincial registry or the state title record.

### What is a lien release letter?

It is a letter from the lender confirming the loan is paid in full and that it is releasing its claim on the vehicle. In Canada the lender should also register a discharge in the provincial registry. In the US the lender signs off on the paper title or sends an electronic release to the state.

Category: Buying

# How to spot a flood-damaged car before you buy (Canada and US)

**A clean title is not a clean car**

Flood brands usually depend on an insurer writing the car off. A car that was never claimed, or that was re-registered somewhere with different rules, can arrive with no brand at all. Run the free checks, then trust what you can see, smell and scan.

A flood-damaged car can look spotless on a lot or in a Marketplace photo. After a hurricane, a spring flood or a storm that fills underground garages, damaged cars need somewhere to go, and some get dried, detailed and listed for sale far from where they flooded, sometimes in another state or across the border in Canada. Here is how to spot one before you pay, which records to check on each side of the border, and what to do if you already bought one.

## Why do flood-damaged cars end up on the used market?

When an insured car floods, the insurer usually writes it off and sells it through a salvage auction. The state or province is then supposed to brand its title so every later buyer knows. Many of those cars are parted out. Some are repaired, legally or otherwise, and sold again.

The trouble starts when the history gets lost. The U.S. Federal Trade Commission warns that storm-damaged cars are sometimes cleaned up and taken out of state for sale. Each state sets its own brands, and the U.S. Department of Justice notes that a car treated as salvage in one place may not carry that brand in another. Moving a car to a state with looser rules and re-titling it there is called **title washing**.

There is also a simpler gap. If the owner had no coverage for the damage, no insurer ever wrote the car off, and no brand was ever applied. That car can look clean on every database.

Why it matters: the FTC notes that water can slowly destroy a car's mechanical and electrical systems and cause rust and corrosion. A flood car can pass a test drive and fail months later, including in safety systems like airbags and ABS that rely on sensors and wiring.

## What are the signs of a flood-damaged car?

Bring a flashlight, see the car in daylight, and give yourself time. No single sign proves a flood, but several together should end the deal.

- **Smell.** A musty, mildew smell, or a heavy perfume of air freshener or cleaning products trying to cover one. Check the trunk too. Close the doors and sit inside for a minute with the heat on.
- **Silt and debris.** Fine mud or sand under the seats, under the dash, in the glovebox, in the spare-tire well and under the trunk floor. Pull a seat belt all the way out: water stains or grit near the end of the webbing are hard to fake away.
- **Rust in odd places.** Rust on seat rails and bolts, pedal brackets, screws under the dash or door hinges on a car that is otherwise in good shape. Interior metal should not rust.
- **Carpet and upholstery.** Carpet that is loose, stained, damp or newer than the rest of the interior. Lift a corner near a door if you can.
- **Lights and glass.** Condensation, fogging or a waterline inside headlights and taillights.
- **Electrical faults.** Test every window, lock, seat motor, mirror, gauge, the radio and screen, the heater and air conditioning. Watch for warning lights that come on and stay on, or that never light up at start-up at all.
- **Engine bay and underbody.** A line of dried debris on the firewall or radiator, mud in crevices, or corrosion on wiring connectors.

**Watch the story too**

A low price, a car recently brought in from a storm-hit region, a seller who won't let you look under the carpet or book an inspection: none of these prove a flood, but they raise the bar for everything else.

## Does a flood car always have a flood title in the US?

No. Use the free and low-cost checks, but read their limits.

**NICB VINCheck.** The National Insurance Crime Bureau runs a free lookup at nicb.org, limited to five searches per IP address in 24 hours. It checks a VIN against theft, salvage and flood records reported by participating member insurers. The FTC points out it only helps if the car was insured when the damage happened.

**NMVTIS.** The National Motor Vehicle Title Information System, reached through vehiclehistory.gov, collects data from state titling agencies, insurers, auto recyclers, and junk and salvage yards. A report covers current title information and brand history (labels such as junk, salvage or flood), the latest odometer reading, and total-loss and salvage records. You buy it through approved private providers, who set their own prices. The Justice Department is clear that not every entity reports yet, so a clean result can be a false negative.

**Tip:** ask to see the actual title, and the previous one if the car was re-titled recently. A fresh title from a different state on a car that just came out of a flood zone deserves a closer look.

## How do Canadian provinces brand flood-damaged cars?

Canada's provinces run their own branding programs, but the flood rule is shared. The Insurance Bureau of Canada says any vehicle flooded to the bottom of the dash must be branded **non-repairable** (also called irreparable), and that every Canadian jurisdiction follows this guideline. Such a vehicle can never be registered for use on a Canadian road.

In Ontario, a written-off car is branded **Salvage** or **Irreparable**, and only vehicles branded **None** or **Rebuilt** can be driven. A car brought in from another province or a U.S. state keeps its brand, except that a Rebuilt brand drops to Salvage until the car passes a structural inspection at a DriveON inspection centre. That carry-over only works if the brand existed in the first place.

Two free or cheap checks help in Canada:

- **IBC VIN Verify** is a free search of vehicles reported as non-repairable in Alberta, Ontario and the Atlantic provinces. IBC notes it may not include every flooded or fire-damaged vehicle.
- **The Ontario UVIP** ($20 from ServiceOntario, and a private seller must give you one) shows the car's brand and Ontario history. Our free VIN check guide explains what else it covers.

## Will a vehicle history report show flood damage?

It may. The FTC says a history report may list accidents and flood damage, but typically won't list mechanical problems. Every report is limited to what its sources reported. A flood that never became an insurance claim, or a repair paid in cash, won't appear anywhere.

Use a report to catch the cars with a recorded past: a total loss, a brand, a gap in registration, or a sudden move from a storm-hit region. Then let the physical checks and the mechanic handle the rest.

## Should you get a mechanic to check for water damage?

Yes, and tell them you're worried about a flood so they look in the right places. A good flood check goes past a test drive:

- scanning every control module for stored fault codes, not just the engine,
- pulling a kick panel or a carpet edge to look at wiring and connectors for green or white corrosion,
- checking engine oil, transmission and differential fluid for a milky look that can mean water got in,
- looking inside the air filter box and around the starter and lower engine for silt,
- checking that the airbag and ABS lights work as they should.

Pay for an inspector who works for you, not the seller. If the seller refuses an inspection, treat that as your answer.

## What if you already bought a flood car?

Stop driving it if warning lights for the airbags, brakes or stability control are on. Then document everything: photos of silt and rust, the mechanic's findings, the ad, messages and the bill of sale.

**In Ontario**, dealers registered with OMVIC must disclose in writing if a vehicle was branded or declared a total loss, and whether it was registered outside Ontario and where. If the contract did not disclose an irreparable, salvage or rebuilt brand, you can cancel within 90 days. OMVIC also notes the Consumer Protection Act can give further rights for misrepresentation for up to one year. Private sales are not covered by OMVIC, so your route there is usually small claims court.

**In the US**, dealers must post a Buyers Guide on every used car saying whether it is sold as is or with a warranty. The FTC suggests reporting a dealer who knowingly sold a storm-damaged or salvage car as sound to the NICB, to ReportFraud.ftc.gov and to your state attorney general.

For a deeper walk through the whole private purchase, from the first message to registration, see our used car buying checklist.

## Common questions

### How can you tell if a used car has flood damage?

Use your nose and a flashlight. Look for a musty smell or heavy air freshener, silt or sand under the seats, in the spare-tire well and along the seat-belt webbing, rust on seat bolts and under the dash, fogged or water-lined lights, and electrical faults. Then run the VIN through the free NICB VINCheck and have a mechanic scan the car.

### Will a VIN check show flood damage?

Sometimes. A VIN check shows flood damage only if it was reported, usually because an insurer wrote the car off or a state or province branded the title. A car that was never claimed, or whose brand was lost when it was re-registered elsewhere, can come back clean.

### Is NICB VINCheck free?

Yes. The National Insurance Crime Bureau's VINCheck is free and limited to five searches per IP address in 24 hours. It looks for theft, salvage and flood records reported by participating insurers, so it only covers cars that were insured when the damage happened.

### Can a flood-damaged car be registered in Canada?

It depends on how deep the water went and how the car was branded. The Insurance Bureau of Canada says a vehicle flooded to the bottom of the dash must be branded non-repairable, also called irreparable, and can never be registered for use on a Canadian road. In Ontario, only vehicles branded None or Rebuilt can be driven.

### Can I return a flood-damaged car I bought from a dealer?

In Ontario, you can cancel a dealer purchase within 90 days if the contract did not disclose in writing that the car was branded irreparable, salvage or rebuilt. In the US, your rights depend on the Buyers Guide and state law, so contact your state attorney general. Private sales offer far less protection.

### How long does flood damage take to show up?

It can take weeks or months. Water left in wiring, connectors and control modules keeps corroding after the car is dried and cleaned, so a flood car can drive normally on a test drive and develop electrical faults later. That is why a scan and a close inspection matter more than a short drive.

## Sources

- How to steer clear of a flood-damaged car - FTC
- Buying a used car from a dealer (Buyers Guide) - FTC
- VINCheck - National Insurance Crime Bureau
- National Motor Vehicle Title Information System (vehiclehistory.gov) - U.S. Department of Justice
- VIN Verify and flood branding - Insurance Bureau of Canada
- Mandatory Vehicle Branding Program - ontario.ca
- Used vehicle information package - ontario.ca
- Disclosures Guideline - OMVIC

URL: https://www.drivee.ca/blog/import-car-from-us-to-canada.html
Category: Buying

# How to import a car from the US to Canada: the 2026 step-by-step guide

**Check the tariff before you buy, not at the border**

Since April 9, 2025, Canada has charged a 25% counter-tariff on passenger vehicles and light trucks from the US, and the relief program is for automakers, not individuals. On a US-built car that can outweigh any saving on the sticker price. Confirm the current rules with the CBSA before you commit.

You can import a car from the US to Canada yourself, without a broker, if you do the steps in the right order: check that Canada accepts the model, file the US export paperwork at least 72 hours ahead, declare the car at the border, then pass a federal inspection and your province's safety check. Here is each step, what it costs, and where people get stuck.

## Can you import a car from the US to Canada?

Usually, yes, but not every car. A vehicle under 15 years old has to meet Canadian safety standards, and Transport Canada keeps a **List of Vehicles Admissible from the United States** through the Registrar of Imported Vehicles (RIV). If the exact make, model and year isn't on the list, or the list says it can't be modified to comply, the car can't come in as a regular import.

Two groups work differently:

- **Vehicles more than 15 years old** (and buses built before January 1, 1971) aren't regulated for import under the Motor Vehicle Safety Act. Age is counted from the month and year of manufacture on the label. Transport Canada notes this doesn't guarantee a province will license it.
- **Vehicles with open safety recalls** need a recall clearance before they can finish the RIV process. RIV accepts a letter on the manufacturer's letterhead stating there are no outstanding recalls, or a printout from an authorized dealer, not a reseller.

## What does it cost to import a car from the US?

Some charges apply to almost every import, and some depend on where the car was built and what it burns. All amounts are in Canadian dollars.

| Charge | Amount | Who it applies to |
| RIV fee | $325 plus GST/PST or HST | Vehicles under 15 years old in the RIV program |
| Customs duty | 0% or 6.1% | 0% if it originates under CUSMA, 6.1% if built outside North America |
| US counter-tariff (surtax) | 25% | Passenger vehicles and light trucks from the US |
| Air conditioning excise tax | $100 | Vehicles with air conditioning |
| Green levy | $1,000 to $4,000 | Passenger cars rated 13 L/100 km or more (weighted) |
| GST | 5% | Collected by the CBSA at the border |
| Provincial sales tax | Varies (8% in Ontario) | Collected by the province at registration |
On top of that you pay for any parts or work needed to pass inspection, the provincial safety check, plates, and a US export agent if you use one. The green levy scale, per the Canada Revenue Agency, is $1,000 from 13 to under 14 L/100 km, rising $1,000 per litre to $4,000 at 16 L/100 km and up.

## Step 1: Check the car before you buy

Most expensive mistakes happen before the car moves. Before you pay a US seller:

1. **Confirm admissibility** on the RIV list for that exact year, make and model.
2. **Check recalls** and ask the seller or a dealer for a recall clearance letter.
3. **Check the title brand.** US states brand titles as salvage, rebuilt, flood and similar. A brand changes the car's value, and you should ask your province's registration office how it treats that brand before you buy.
4. **Check for a lien.** If a lender is on the title, US Customs needs a letter from the lienholder authorizing export.
5. **Note the country of manufacture.** The first character of the VIN tells you where it was built: 1, 4 or 5 for the US, 2 for Canada, 3 for Mexico. That drives duty and the surtax.

**Tip:** a US history report is your best defence against flood cars and rolled-back odometers that get washed through state lines. A clean ad is not a clean title.

## Step 2: US export and the 72-hour rule

The US side is where most first-time importers get turned back. Under US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) rules for used vehicles crossing by land, **the required documents must be submitted to CBP at least 72 hours before export**, and the vehicle must be presented to CBP when it leaves. RIV's own guidance is to send them at least three business days ahead.

What you'll need:

- the **original certificate of title** (or a certified copy) plus two complete copies,
- a bill of sale,
- a letter from the lienholder or lessor if the title shows one,
- an **ITN** (Internal Transaction Number) from an electronic export filing in the US Automated Export System (AES). RIV notes this is usually filed by a US freight forwarder or broker, and the car must be on US soil when the filing is made and throughout the export.

Export offices keep their own hours, and many close on weekends and holidays. Call the specific port before you drive there.

## Step 3: Declare it at the Canadian border

At the Canadian side, you tell the Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA) you're importing the car. The CBSA completes the **Vehicle Import Form, Form 1**, or issues a paperless release by email. Keep it. Your province will ask for it, with the federal stamps, before it registers the car.

You pay the GST, any duty, surtax and excise tax to the CBSA at the border. The RIV fee is paid to the RIV after you cross. RIV says the amount appears at the bottom of the paper Form 1 or in the CBSA release email, and a late-payment notice goes out automatically if it isn't paid online within 10 days of import.

**Bring originals**

Have the title, bill of sale, recall letter and ITN with you, plus proof of the price you paid. The CBSA calculates duty and tax on the value of the car, converted to Canadian dollars.

## Is there duty or a tariff on a US car?

Two separate charges can apply, and people often mix them up.

**Customs duty.** A vehicle that qualifies as originating under CUSMA (the Canada-United States-Mexico Agreement, called USMCA in the US) generally enters duty-free. A car built outside North America, such as a German- or Japanese-built model bought from a US dealer, pays 6.1%.

**The 25% counter-tariff.** Since April 9, 2025, Canada has applied a 25% surtax on passenger vehicles and light trucks from the US. According to the federal government's April 2026 notice:

- for a US vehicle that is **not** CUSMA-compliant, the surtax is charged on the full value for duty, on top of any regular duty,
- for a **CUSMA-compliant** US vehicle, the share of value made up of Canadian and Mexican parts is excluded, and that content is assumed to be 15% unless you prove more,
- the remission (relief) program, renewed to April 8, 2027, gives eligible **automakers** a set number of surtax-free vehicles. It is not something a private importer can claim.

In practice that means a US-built car can owe a surtax of roughly 21% of its value before GST. Trade measures between the two countries have changed several times since 2025, so check the CBSA's current customs notices in the week you buy.

## Step 4: The RIV inspection within 45 days

Once the car is in Canada, a vehicle in the RIV program needs a **federal RIV inspection within 45 days** of the declaration, at an authorized inspection centre. RIV lists the locations. The inspection checks that the car was modified, where needed, to meet Canadian standards and that recalls are cleared.

Don't let the deadline slide. RIV warns that failing to pass within the required time leads to non-compliance, which can be enforced with fines, penalties and removal of the vehicle under the Motor Vehicle Safety Act. Book the inspection as soon as your RIV fee is paid and any modifications are done.

## Step 5: Provincial safety and registration

Registration is provincial, so the details vary. In Ontario, for a car from outside Canada, you register in person at a ServiceOntario centre and bring:

- the Vehicle Import Form 1, with both stamps showing it met federal requirements,
- the original US title,
- a **Safety Standards Certificate** from a licensed inspection station. You can register without one, but you can't put plates on the car until you have it,
- proof of Ontario insurance.

Ontario also collects the 8% provincial portion of the HST at ServiceOntario when the CBSA has already charged the 5% GST. Other provinces have their own inspection and tax rules, so check before the car arrives.

## Is it still worth importing a car from the US?

For a car built in Canada or Mexico, or a vehicle over 15 years old, the math can still work. For a recent US-built car, add the 25% surtax, GST, provincial tax, the RIV fee, any modifications and your travel, then compare that total with the same car for sale in Canada. Price it against Canadian listings, not against the US sticker.

## Common questions

### How much does it cost to import a car from the US to Canada?

For most vehicles under 15 years old you pay the $325 RIV fee plus tax, 5% GST at the border, a $100 excise tax if the car has air conditioning, and provincial sales tax at registration. Depending on the car you may also owe 6.1% duty, the 25% counter-tariff on US vehicles and the green levy of $1,000 to $4,000 for fuel-inefficient models. Shipping, export agent, modification and inspection costs are extra.

### Do I pay duty on a car bought in the US?

Not if it qualifies as originating under CUSMA, which generally covers vehicles built in Canada, the US or Mexico. A car built elsewhere, such as a German- or Japanese-built model bought in the US, pays 6.1% duty. Duty is separate from the 25% counter-tariff on US vehicles.

### Is there a tariff on US cars coming into Canada in 2026?

Yes, as of the latest federal notices. Since April 9, 2025, Canada has applied a 25% counter-tariff on passenger vehicles and light trucks from the US. For CUSMA-compliant vehicles it is charged on the value minus Canadian and Mexican content, assumed to be 15% unless you prove more. The relief program is for automakers, not private importers, so check with the CBSA before you buy.

### Can I drive a car from the US to Canada myself?

Yes. Many people drive the car to the border themselves. You still need to submit the export documents to US Customs and Border Protection at least 72 hours before you cross, present the car at the US export office, then declare it to the CBSA on the Canadian side. Make sure it is insured and legally plated for the drive.

### What happens if I miss the 45-day RIV inspection?

RIV warns that failing to pass the federal inspection within the required time leads to non-compliance, which can be enforced with fines, penalties and removal of the vehicle under the Motor Vehicle Safety Act. Without the completed federal paperwork, your province will not register the car either.

### Can I import a car that is more than 15 years old?

Yes. Vehicles manufactured more than 15 years ago, counted by month and year of manufacture, are not regulated for import under the Motor Vehicle Safety Act, so they skip the RIV program. You still follow the US export rules, pay any duty and taxes that apply, and pass your province's safety inspection.

## Sources

- Importing a vehicle from the United States and Mexico - Transport Canada
- FAQ: importing vehicles purchased in the United States - Transport Canada
- Vehicle admissibility - Registrar of Imported Vehicles
- Recall clearance - Registrar of Imported Vehicles
- AES and CBP export requirements - Registrar of Imported Vehicles
- Federal RIV inspection - Registrar of Imported Vehicles
- Exporting a motor vehicle - U.S. Customs and Border Protection
- Memorandum D19-12-1: Importing vehicles into Canada - CBSA
- Customs Notice 20-26: RIV program fee - CBSA
- Customs Notice 26-10: United States Surtax Remission Order (Motor Vehicles 2026) - CBSA
- United States Surtax Remission Order (Motor Vehicles 2026) - Canada Gazette
- Current rates of excise taxes (A/C and fuel-inefficient vehicles) - CRA
- HST: motor vehicles, boats and aircraft - ontario.ca

Category: Buying

# Odometer rollback: how to spot it and what to do

**The number on the dash is not proof**

Odometer rollback is still a real risk with digital clusters, because the tools to reprogram them are easy to buy. Check the car’s wear against its mileage, line up every recorded reading, and get recourse lined up before you pay, not after. Buyers from private sellers have far fewer protections than buyers from licensed dealers.

Odometer rollback means changing a car’s odometer so it shows fewer kilometres or miles than the car has actually travelled. It inflates the price and hides wear, and it hasn’t gone away just because odometers went digital. Here is how odometer rollback works today, how to spot it on the car and in the paperwork, and what you can do about it in Canada and the United States.

## How does digital odometer rollback work?

Older mechanical odometers were turned back by physically spinning the gears, which often left scratches, loose screws or digits that didn’t line up. Modern odometers store mileage electronically, so a rollback is done by reprogramming the instrument cluster or the module that holds the reading. Ontario’s dealer regulator, OMVIC, notes that devices capable of reprogramming odometers are readily available.

A digital rollback can leave nothing visible on the dash. That is why the reliable checks are indirect: wear that doesn’t match the mileage, and recorded readings that don’t add up. On many modern cars, mileage is also stored in other control modules, so a dealer or technician with the right scan tool may find a reading that doesn’t match the cluster.

## How can you tell if an odometer has been rolled back?

Start with the car itself. Official guidance from OMVIC and the Government of Alberta points to the same warning signs:

- **Wear that doesn’t fit the mileage.** A worn or shiny steering wheel, worn driver’s seat bolsters, tired carpets and floor mats, or worn door strikers on a car that is supposed to be lightly used.
- **Worn pedal pads.** Rubber on the brake, gas or clutch pedal worn smooth or through.
- **A pitted windshield.** A sand-blasted look from years of highway driving.
- **Worn suspension parts** beyond what the mileage would explain.
- **Oil change stickers and service records** with dates or readings that don’t match the odometer.
- **Signs of tampering on older cars:** misaligned digits, a trip odometer that doesn’t work, missing dash screws or scratches near the cluster.
- **An unusually low reading for the age.** Alberta’s guidance flags less than 20,000 km a year (about 12,400 miles) as unusually low and worth a closer look.

Watch the seller too. OMVIC lists meeting in a parking lot instead of at home, discouraging a history report or inspection, a name that doesn’t match the ownership, a price well below market and a demand for cash as common red flags.

**Tip:** low mileage on its own isn’t proof of anything. Plenty of cars really are driven very little. The red flag is low mileage plus wear, records or a story that don’t fit.

## How do you check a car’s mileage records?

Collect every reading you can find, with dates, and put them in order. The mileage should only go up, at a pace that makes sense for the car’s use.

- **Ontario UVIP.** The $20 package from ServiceOntario lists each Ontario owner along with an odometer reading. OMVIC notes these readings are unverified, so small differences are normal (the UVIP may show slightly more than the dash because of reporting timing). A large drop is not. Order your own copy, because OMVIC also warns that some sellers have altered a UVIP to remove odometer or lien information.
- **Alberta Vehicle Information Report.** Includes the odometer reading if one was provided. Alberta notes that reporting a reading is voluntary, so it may be missing.
- **US title and NMVTIS.** The US title carries the odometer disclosure made at each transfer. An NMVTIS report shows the latest reported odometer reading.
- **A full vehicle history report.** Pulls readings from registrations, inspections, emissions tests and service visits across provinces and states into one timeline.
- **The car’s own paperwork.** Service invoices, safety inspection reports and dealer work orders usually record the mileage. Ask for them.

A later reading that is lower than an earlier one is the clearest sign of a rollback or a replaced cluster. A long stretch where the mileage barely moves while the car keeps being registered and serviced is the second.

## Kilometres vs miles on cross-border cars

Cars move between Canada and the US all the time, and unit mix-ups are a common source of false alarms, and real fraud. One mile is about 1.609 km. A car that shows 60,000 miles in US records has about 96,500 km on it.

- If a US record in miles is read as kilometres, the mileage seems to jump when the car arrives in Canada, which is harmless.
- If a Canadian reading in kilometres is later entered as miles, or a cluster is swapped to a different unit, the car can look like it has far less on it than it does.

**Tip:** for any car with a US past, convert every reading into one unit before comparing. Check whether the dash is set to km or miles, and whether the cluster looks original.

## What does US law say about odometer rollback?

Federal law, in 49 U.S.C. Chapter 327, makes it illegal to disconnect, reset or alter an odometer intending to change the mileage, and to sell or fit a device that makes an odometer show the wrong mileage. If an odometer is repaired or replaced and can’t keep the same reading, it must be set to zero and a notice attached to the left door frame showing the mileage before the work and the date.

**Odometer disclosure.** Under federal rules (49 CFR Part 580), a seller must state the mileage in writing when ownership is transferred and certify one of three things: the reading is the actual mileage, the mileage exceeds the odometer’s mechanical limits, or the reading is not the actual mileage and should not be relied on. The disclosure is usually made on the title itself.

**The 20-year disclosure rule**

NHTSA extended the disclosure exemption from 10 to 20 model years. Vehicles from model year 2010 and older stay under the old 10-year exemption and no longer need a disclosure. Model year 2011 and newer must be disclosed until they are 20 model years old, so a 2011 model becomes exempt in 2031. Vehicles with a gross vehicle weight rating over 16,000 pounds are also exempt. Some states apply their own rules on top.

**Recourse.** A buyer can sue anyone who violated the federal odometer law with intent to defraud for three times the actual damages or $10,000, whichever is greater, plus costs and a reasonable attorney’s fee if they win. The lawsuit must be filed within two years after the claim arises. NHTSA advises reporting tampering to your state’s motor vehicle enforcement authority and, if a dealer was involved, to the state agency that licenses dealers. NHTSA itself investigates large-scale odometer fraud.

## What are the odometer rules in Canada?

In Canada, used car sales are regulated by the provinces, so the protection you get depends mostly on where you bought and who you bought from.

### Ontario

- **Registered dealers.** If an OMVIC-registered dealer fails to disclose that the odometer doesn’t reflect the vehicle’s true distance travelled, the buyer can cancel the contract within 90 days of delivery. Complaints go to OMVIC.
- **Compensation Fund.** When a registered dealer is out of business or won’t resolve a proven loss, OMVIC’s Compensation Fund may pay eligible buyers up to $45,000 per transaction. It doesn’t cover private sales.
- **Private sellers and curbsiders.** OMVIC can’t help with a private purchase. The usual remedy is to find the seller and sue. Ontario’s Small Claims Court hears claims up to $50,000, a limit in place since October 1, 2025.

### Alberta and British Columbia

The Government of Alberta states that odometer tampering is illegal in Alberta, even on an “as is” sale, and lists the Alberta Motor Vehicle Industry Council (AMVIC) as the body that may investigate an odometer complaint. It also suggests a police report and, if the seller won’t refund you, a court claim. In British Columbia, dealers are regulated by the Vehicle Sales Authority of BC.

**Tip:** buying from a licensed dealer doesn’t make rollback impossible, but it gives you a regulator and, in Ontario, a fund to fall back on. With a private sale, your protection is the checking you do before you pay.

## What should you do if you bought a car with a rolled-back odometer?

1. **Gather the evidence.** Every report, the UVIP or title, the bill of sale, the ad (screenshot it before it disappears), messages with the seller and photos of the dash.
2. **Get a written opinion.** Ask a dealer for that brand or an independent mechanic to scan the modules and note the wear in writing.
3. **Contact the seller in writing.** Ask for the contract to be cancelled, or for the difference in value.
4. **Escalate.** In Canada, a dealer purchase goes to the provincial regulator (OMVIC, AMVIC or the VSA). In the US, go to the state motor vehicle agency or the dealer licensing agency.
5. **Consider police and court.** If you believe you were deliberately deceived, report it to local police. For money, use small claims or civil court, or in the US a federal odometer claim within the two-year limit.

Act quickly. The Ontario dealer window is 90 days from delivery, and a US federal odometer claim must be filed within two years after it arises.

## Common questions

### How can you tell if an odometer has been rolled back?

Compare the wear with the mileage and line up every recorded reading. Worn pedals, a shiny steering wheel, worn seats and a pitted windshield on a low-mileage car are warning signs. So is any record where a later odometer reading is lower than an earlier one.

### Can a digital odometer be rolled back?

Yes. Digital odometers store mileage electronically, and reprogramming tools are readily available. A digital rollback can leave no visible marks, so history records, service paperwork and a mechanic’s inspection matter more than the dash itself.

### Is odometer rollback illegal?

Yes. In the US, federal law prohibits altering an odometer to change the mileage, and victims can sue for three times their damages or $10,000, whichever is greater. In Canada the rules are provincial. Alberta, for example, states that tampering is illegal, and Ontario dealers must disclose when an odometer does not show the true distance.

### What can I do if a private seller sold me a car with a rolled-back odometer?

Dealer regulators such as OMVIC do not cover private sales, so the usual remedy is to contact the seller in writing and, if that fails, sue. In Ontario, Small Claims Court hears claims up to $50,000. You can also report deliberate fraud to local police.

### Does a vehicle history report show odometer rollback?

It can show the signs. A report lists odometer readings recorded at registrations, inspections and service visits, and a later reading that is lower than an earlier one is a strong warning. It cannot catch a rollback made between two records that were never reported.

### Do US sellers still have to disclose mileage on older cars?

For model year 2011 and newer vehicles, yes, until the vehicle is 20 model years old. Model year 2010 and older vehicles remain under the old 10-year exemption and no longer need a federal odometer disclosure.

## Sources

Category: Buying

# Salvage vs rebuilt title: what it means before you buy (Canada and US)

**Rebuilt means inspected, not like new**

A rebuilt car passed an inspection on the day it was inspected. That does not prove every repair was done well, and the brand stays on the record. Price it, insure it and inspect it as the written-off car it once was.

A salvage title means an insurer or owner declared the car a total loss. A rebuilt title means that same car was repaired and passed an inspection to go back on the road. That is the short answer to salvage vs rebuilt title in both Canada and the US. The details depend on where the car was branded, and brands do not always survive a trip across a state, provincial or national border.

## What is a salvage title?

A **salvage** brand marks a vehicle that was written off. Usually an insurer paid out the claim as a total loss after a collision, fire, flood or theft, and decided repairs would cost too much relative to the car's value.

In the US, each state issues its own titles and sets its own rules, so the trigger for a salvage title and the exact wording on it vary from state to state. What is common is the result: a salvage vehicle generally can't be registered or driven on public roads until it is repaired and passes a state inspection. Texas, for example, says a salvage vehicle can't be registered or driven until it passes a Texas safety inspection and receives a "Rebuilt Salvage" title.

Canada has no US-style certificate of title. Each province records the brand, often called a status, on its vehicle registration record. In Ontario the brand appears on the vehicle permit, in the Used Vehicle Information Package (UVIP) and in the ministry's registration system.

## Salvage vs rebuilt title: what is a rebuilt title?

A **rebuilt** brand goes on a salvage vehicle that has been repaired and has passed the required inspection. It tells the next buyer the car was a total loss that has since been certified for the road.

The name changes by jurisdiction. Texas issues a "Rebuilt Salvage" title. California calls it **revived salvage**, which its DMV defines as a salvage vehicle that was repaired and reregistered.

In Ontario, getting from Salvage to Rebuilt takes a **structural inspection** at a specialized DriveON Vehicle Inspection Centre. The owner has to provide photos of the car in its damaged state, documents and detailed invoices for major parts used in the rebuild. To register and plate the car you need both a Structural Inspection Certificate and a Safety Standards Certificate, and the brand changes to Rebuilt once the structural certificate is submitted at ServiceOntario.

**Tip:** ask the seller of a rebuilt car for that rebuild file: the damage photos, parts invoices and inspection certificate. A seller who rebuilt the car properly usually has it. One who can't produce any of it is telling you something.

## What other title brands should you watch for in the US?

Salvage and rebuilt are the best known, but they are not the only brands. The California DMV lists brands commonly used across states, including:

- **Junk** or **nonrepairable**: for parts or scrap. In Texas, a nonrepairable vehicle can't be repaired, rebuilt or made operable for public roads.
- **Water damage** or **flood**: damaged by water. Flood cars can hide corrosion and electrical problems that show up months later.
- **Lemon law buyback** or **warranty returned**: bought back by the manufacturer under a state lemon law.
- **Dismantled**, **totaled**, **scrap vehicle** and **revived junk**.
- **Prior taxi**, **prior police** and **gray market**: not damage, but worth knowing.

Because each state defines its own brands, a flood brand in one state does not automatically become a flood brand in the next. That gap is where title washing starts, covered below.

## How do Canadian provinces brand written-off cars?

Each province runs its own program. The four largest look like this:

| Province | Written off, can be repaired | Repaired and inspected | Parts or scrap only |
| Ontario (MTO) | Salvage | Rebuilt | Irreparable |
| British Columbia (ICBC) | Salvage | Rebuilt | Non-repairable |
| Alberta | Salvage | Rebuilt | Non-repairable |
| Quebec (SAAQ) | Severely damaged | Rebuilt | Irreparable |
**Ontario.** The Mandatory Vehicle Branding Program has four brands: None, Salvage, Rebuilt and Irreparable. Only None and Rebuilt vehicles can be driven on Ontario roads. Brands can be assigned by the ministry, insurers, auto recyclers, salvagers, auctioneers, dealers and owners. An Irreparable vehicle can never be driven in Ontario again.

**British Columbia.** ICBC's statuses are normal, salvage, rebuilt, altered and non-repairable. A rebuilt status goes to a salvage vehicle after repair and inspection. A non-repairable vehicle can never be re-licensed or insured.

**Alberta.** A salvage vehicle can't be registered. It needs a Salvage Vehicle Inspection at a licensed Alberta inspection facility to become rebuilt, and the province says the inspection certificate must be presented at a registry within 14 days or the car needs a full inspection again. Alberta says the rebuilt status follows the vehicle for the rest of its useful life. A non-repairable vehicle can never be registered and can only be sold as scrap or for parts.

**Quebec.** The SAAQ gives a car that needs rebuilding a "severely damaged" status. Until it is rebuilt it can't be driven on public roads, only towed or transported. It has to pass a technical appraisal and a mechanical inspection before it gets a rebuilt status. Since January 1, 2025, rebuilders also have to show proof that driver assistance systems were recalibrated. Flooded vehicles get an irreparable status, which is final.

## What happens to a brand when a car crosses a border?

**Between US states.** The US Department of Justice warns that brand washing can happen when a car is retitled in another state. The National Motor Vehicle Title Information System (NMVTIS) exists to close that gap. It is the only vehicle history database in the US that all states, insurers and junk and salvage yards are required by federal law to report to.

**From the US into Canada.** Transport Canada lists vehicles branded junk, scrap, parts-only, non-repairable, flood or water damage as inadmissible for import as a salvage vehicle meant for the road. Those can come in only for parts, and a vehicle declared parts-only at import is given a non-repairable status that the Registrar of Imported Vehicles reports to every province and territory.

**Into Ontario from anywhere else.** Ontario keeps a brand from another Canadian province or US state, with one twist: a car branded Rebuilt elsewhere is branded Salvage when it is registered in Ontario. It needs an Ontario structural inspection before it can be registered as Rebuilt and driven.

**From Canada into the US.** NMVTIS is built on US state, insurer and salvage-yard reports. A brand recorded only by a Canadian province may not show up there, so a US buyer looking at a former Canadian car should also check the provincial record or a report that covers Canadian data.

## Is a rebuilt title car worth buying?

It can be, if the price reflects the brand, the repair was done properly, and you can insure and eventually sell it.

- **Insurance.** Coverage on branded cars is up to each insurer. Some will ask for the inspection paperwork or limit physical damage coverage. Get a quote on the actual VIN before you buy.
- **Financing.** Some lenders won't finance branded vehicles at all. If you need a loan, ask your lender first.
- **Resale.** The brand stays on the record, and the next buyer will see it in the same places you did. Expect to sell at a discount too.
- **The repair itself.** An inspection certificate is a minimum, not a warranty. Have your own mechanic look at frame rails, panel gaps, airbag and seatbelt warnings, signs of water in the cabin, and whether driver assistance sensors work.

## How do I check if a car has a salvage or rebuilt title?

1. **Read the paperwork.** In the US, the brand is printed on the title. In Ontario, check the vehicle permit and the UVIP, which a private seller is legally required to give you. Our free VIN check guide explains what the $20 UVIP covers.
2. **US records.** Get an NMVTIS report through an approved provider listed at vehiclehistory.gov. It shows the current title, brand history, the latest odometer reading and total-loss reports. The National Insurance Crime Bureau's free VINCheck can flag vehicles reported as salvage or stolen by participating insurers.
3. **Provincial records.** In BC, ICBC sells a vehicle claims history search. In Alberta, any registry agent sells a Vehicle Information Report showing status. In Quebec, the status appears on the registration certificate, and the ownership history you can get through SAAQclic shows it.
4. **A cross-border report.** If the car has lived in more than one state or province, a history report that covers Canadian and US data is the easiest way to catch a brand that was left behind. The Drivee Car Report works for any North American VIN.
5. **An inspection.** No record shows a repair that was done for cash and never reported.

For the full private-sale process in Ontario, from the UVIP to the bill of sale, see our used car buying checklist.

## Common questions

### What is the difference between a salvage and a rebuilt title?

A salvage title or brand means the car was written off as a total loss and is not yet approved for the road. A rebuilt title or brand means that salvage car was repaired and passed the required inspection, so it can be registered and driven again. The rebuilt brand stays on the record.

### Can you drive a car with a salvage title?

Generally no. In Ontario only vehicles branded None or Rebuilt can be driven, and Alberta will not register a salvage vehicle. US states generally require repair and inspection before a salvage vehicle can be registered. You can usually tow or transport it to a repair shop or inspection station.

### Can a rebuilt title go back to a clean title?

Not legitimately in the jurisdictions covered here. The rebuilt brand records past damage and stays with the car; Alberta, for one, says it follows the vehicle for the rest of its useful life. Ontario lets an owner contest only a Salvage or Irreparable brand assigned in Ontario, within 90 days and while the car is unrepaired. A former rebuilt car showing a clean title after a move is a reason to dig deeper.

### Is it worth buying a car with a rebuilt title?

It can be, if the price reflects the brand, the repair was done properly and you can insure and finance it. Get an insurance quote on the VIN, ask for the rebuild photos, invoices and inspection certificate, and have your own mechanic inspect it before you pay.

### How do I find out if a car has a salvage title?

Check the title in the US or the vehicle permit and UVIP in Ontario, then confirm with an independent record: an NMVTIS report in the US, the provincial record in Canada, or a history report that covers both countries for a car that has crossed borders.

### Can I import a salvage title car from the US into Canada?

Some salvage vehicles can be imported for road use, but Transport Canada lists vehicles branded junk, scrap, parts-only, non-repairable, flood or water damage as inadmissible for that. They can only come in for parts and get a permanent non-repairable status. Provinces also apply their own rules, such as Ontario's structural inspection.
